title: Ovarian Torsion
sources: Critical Vector — OB Pocket Guide: Ovarian Torsion (ACOG 2023)
ACOG Committee Opinion, Adnexal Torsion in Adolescents

changelog.change: Initial entry — presentation, ultrasound findings + the Doppler caveat, and the diagnostic/surgical steps table.

summary: A time-critical surgical emergency. A normal Doppler does NOT rule it out — clinical suspicion drives the decision to operate. Do not withhold analgesia pending the diagnosis. Detorse even a blue-black ovary; reserve oophorectomy for confirmed necrosis.

body.text: Delay beyond 6–8 hours substantially increases the risk of ovarian necrosis and loss. Suspicion plus a supportive picture is enough to go to laparoscopy — do not wait for a 'positive' Doppler.

items: Acute-onset severe unilateral pelvic / lower abdominal pain (often 8–10/10), frequently colicky.
Nausea / vomiting in ~ 70% — a prominent feature; may mimic appendicitis.
Pain may be intermittent early (intermittent torsion with spontaneous detorsion).
Low-grade fever if necrosis is developing.
Predisposing: ovarian cyst / mass ≥ 5 cm (corpus luteum, dermoid, endometrioma), OHSS, pregnancy.
Enlarged ovary (> 4 cm) with follicles displaced to the periphery — the 'string of pearls' sign.
Ovarian stromal oedema / heterogeneity on grayscale.
Absent or diminished Doppler flow — sensitivity only 60–74%; a normal Doppler does NOT exclude torsion.
Free fluid in the cul-de-sac; an associated cyst or mass.

rows: Morphine 4–8 mg IV + ketorolac 30 mg IV
Do NOT withhold — opioids do not mask the exam in modern practice
CBC, BMP, β-hCG, LDH; tumour markers (CA-125, AFP, β-hCG) if a mass
Rule out ruptured ectopic; characterise a mass preoperatively
Detorse first even if discoloured — a black/blue ovary may recover. Oophorectomy only for confirmed necrosis
For high recurrence risk or a single remaining ovary
